pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: The triad of severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical exam, acute neuropsychiatric decline with motor neuropathy, and urine darkening to a port-wine hue upon light exposure—catastrophically precipitated and worsened by CYP450-inducing triggers (sulfonamides, starvation/keto diet, and phenytoin). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is an autosomal dominant metabolic disorder caused by a partial deficiency of the heme biosynthesis enzyme hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS, also known as porphobilinogen deaminase). Under metabolic triggers—such as caloric deprivation (fasting) or drugs that induce hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (sulfamethoxazole, phenytoin)—cellular heme demands surge, upregulating the rate-limiting enzyme delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1). Due to the downstream enzyme block, neurotoxic heme precursors (delta-aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen) accumulate exponentially. These precursors cause widespread autonomic neuropathy (severe colicky pain, tachycardia, hypertension), central nervous system toxicity (psychosis, seizures, SIADH-induced hyponatremia), and peripheral motor neuropathy (flaccid quadriparesis and wrist/foot drops). Sunlight/air oxidation polymerizes porphobilinogen into porphobilin and porphyrins, turning the urine a pathognomonic dark red or port-wine color. Definitive management requires immediate cessation of inducing agents, administration of IV dextrose, and IV hemin to downregulate ALAS1.
